11.t: Working with data: Arctic sea ice
q: Calculate the percentage fall in September sea ice from 1980 to 2020.
Calculate the mean loss per decade.
3.8 / 4 = about 0.95 million km² per decade.
2012 is far below the trend. Explain why a single year should not be used to judge a trend.
Ice extent varies from year to year with weather and winds; a trend needs many years of data.
Explain how the loss of sea ice speeds up warming.
Ice is white and reflects most sunlight (high albedo). Open ocean is dark and absorbs it, warming the water and melting more ice: positive feedback.
Name a species at risk from loss of sea ice, and explain why.
Polar bear: it hunts seals from the ice, so less ice means less food. (Or walrus, seals, ice algae.)

16.t: Working with data: species moving uphill
q: Calculate the mean rate at which the butterfly’s upper limit moved, in metres per decade.
(1880 − 1650) / 4.5 decades = about 51 m per decade.
Suggest why the butterfly’s range is moving uphill.
Warmer temperatures: the zone of suitable climate (and its food plants) is shifting to higher altitude.
The plant moves more slowly than the butterfly. Suggest why, and one consequence.
Plants spread only by seeds and grow slowly. The butterfly may move away from its food plants, causing a mismatch.
Predict when the plant will reach the summit if the trend continues, and explain the risk.
About 2 m per year, 15 m to go: around 2033. It then has nowhere higher to go, so it may die out on this mountain.
Explain why species on mountain tops are most at risk.
They cannot move higher, their habitat area shrinks towards the summit, and populations are small and isolated.

21.t: Working with data: bleaching and temperature
q: Describe the relationship for typical corals.
Little bleaching below 1 °C, then it rises steeply: 45% at 2 °C and 80% at 3 °C.
Explain why bleaching harms corals.
Under heat stress corals expel their algae (zooxanthellae), which supply most of their food from photosynthesis. Without them the corals starve, and they die if the heat lasts.
Compare the two kinds of reef and suggest the advantage of heat-tolerant algae.
Less bleaching at every temperature (20% against 45% at 2 °C): the algae stay in the coral at higher temperatures.
Predict the effect of very hot years every 2 to 3 years.
Reefs need about 10 years to recover, so they would not recover between events: coral would die and reef species would be lost.
Suggest how heat-tolerant corals could become more common.
By natural selection, as heat kills the less tolerant corals (or by people breeding and planting them).
